content.text:
The biggest remaining “cheap” actions are the ones that consume valuable resources or create permanent power, but resolve in one interaction tick.

Recent progress covered eating, fishing, and selected spell casts. The next obvious targets are:

- **Cooking** — currently consumes ingredients and creates food immediately in [cookingGame.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/content/cooking/cookingGame.js). Make it a 3–6 turn channel, interrupted by movement or damage.
- **Applying enchantments** — scrolls immediately attach permanent runtime topology in [scrolls.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/content/items/scrolls.js). This is probably the highest-value missing delay: 2–3 turns, interrupted by movement/damage.
- **Crafting enchant scrolls** — the bench consumes reagents and produces the scroll immediately in [benchGame.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/content/enchanting/benchGame.js). 4–8 turns would make the station feel like a commitment.
- **Alchemy/brewing** — same issue: ingredients vanish and potions appear immediately. 3–5 turns.
- **Smelting, forging, and milling** — these already animate the workstation for a few turns, but the actual reward is granted immediately in [interactPayloads.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/content/interaction/interactPayloads.js). The animation currently communicates “work happened” after the fact; the player should be occupied during it.
- **Harvesting** — tool and stamina costs are real, but the resource appears immediately. 1–2 turns would make harvesting under threat meaningful.
- **Lockpicking** — the prompt/minigame is present, but the attempt itself should probably consume 2–4 turns, with failure still costing time.
- **Drinking potions** — [drinkSystem.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/drinkSystem.js) resolves them immediately. A 1-turn delay would make emergency healing and buffing a tactical decision.
- **Applying oils, gems, repair tools, and other item upgrades** — the generic apply path in [applySystem.js](/home/pjensen/Repos/JSHack/src/rules/systems/applySystem.js) is another likely “instant power” bucket. Usually 1–3 turns.
- **Praying/offering at altars** — especially offerings that consume an item and grant a major blessing. These should feel like a deliberate ritual, perhaps 2–5 turns.

I would leave these instant:

- reading, inspecting, talking, and opening menus;
- toggling lanterns/doors where there is no meaningful exposure;
- picking up ordinary loot;
- opening a UI without actually committing to a craft;
- minor interface choices.

The cleanest next implementation slice is a generic “committed action” channel for workstation operations and item application. That would let cooking, enchanting, brewing, smelting, and applying scrolls share the same interruption/progress behavior that eating already established, instead of each inventing its own timing system.
pick one and make it happen please -- use color, use text "Cooking" as a good first example.

I’ll make cooking the first committed workstation action: selecting a recipe will start a visible “Cooking” channel, consume ingredients and produce the meal only when the channel completes, and movement/damage will interrupt it. I’m checking the existing channel lifecycle and cooking UI dispatch now so the change stays on the canonical interaction path. I’m also using the repo’s agent-tools guidance to verify the affected boundaries before editing.
